title: How to Recognize Phishing
summary: Urgent messages that imitate a trusted organization are a common way to steal passwords.
content: Phishing messages try to trick people into revealing passwords, payment details, or other private information. Attackers may use urgent language, suspicious links, or messages that imitate a campus, bank, or lecturer. A report in CyberAware records the message. It does not prove that an attack succeeded.

title: Protecting an Account
summary: A unique password and a second sign-in check reduce the impact of a leaked password.
content: Reusing one password across services increases risk if one service is compromised. Unexpected password-reset mail and sign-in alerts from an unknown place should be reported, then checked through the official account page rather than through the message itself.

title: Understanding Malware
summary: Unexpected attachments, double extensions, and scare pop-ups are reasons to stop and report.
content: Malware is software that a person did not intend to run. A file named like a document but ending in an executable extension, a USB installer from an unknown source, or a pop-up that demands a phone call should not be opened. Report the file name and where it came from.

title: Signs of Unauthorized Access
summary: Unknown sessions, changed files, and mail the owner did not send need a review.
content: Unauthorized access means someone used an account, mailbox, or shared folder without permission. Signs include a new device in the session list, files renamed overnight, or mail sent from a shared mailbox that the usual owners did not write. Change the password only through the official site after the report is filed.

title: Other Social Engineering Tricks
summary: Phone calls, QR posters, and public Wi-Fi prompts can ask for information that should stay private.
content: Not every report fits phishing, malware, or an account alert. A caller asking for a payment code, a QR poster that does not match the official site, or a cafe Wi-Fi page that asks for a certificate should be reported with what was asked and whether anything was opened or installed.
